Compare the three families of 2D transformations (linear, affine, projective) in terms of matrix form, properties, and what they preserve.
risposta: Linear transformations are 2x2 matrices (scale, rotation, shear); they keep the origin fixed, map lines to lines, keep parallel lines parallel and length ratios preserved, and are closed under composition - but cannot represent translation, which moves the origin. Affine transformations use homogeneous coordinates and a 3x3 matrix with last row [0 0 1], combining linear maps and translation; the origin need not map to the origin but other linear properties hold (lines, parallelism, ratios). Projective transformations (homographies) are general 3x3 matrices defined up to scale, mapping one plane to another; parallel lines may converge to a vanishing point and ratios are not preserved, though lines still map to lines.

domanda: Explain how to compute a transformation from point correspondences, including least squares and the special handling of a homography.
risposta: Each correspondence gives equations in the unknown matrix entries. A 2D linear transform has 4 unknowns (>=2 matches), an affine 6 unknowns (>=3 matches), a homography 8 independent unknowns (>=4 matches). With more matches you get an overdetermined system At=b solved by least squares via the normal equations t=(A^T A)^{-1} A^T b. A homography instead leads to a homogeneous system Ah=0 (since it is defined up to scale); this is a constrained problem, minimize ||Ah||^2 subject to ||h||=1, whose solution is the eigenvector of A^T A with the smallest eigenvalue (via SVD).

domanda: Explain RANSAC for robust transformation estimation and why it is needed.
risposta: Least squares is sensitive to outliers (wrong feature matches), which can ruin the fit. RANSAC is iterative: (1) randomly sample the minimal number of points needed (2 linear, 3 affine, 4 homography); (2) compute the model from that minimal sample; (3) count inliers within tolerance epsilon; (4) repeat for N iterations and keep the model with the most inliers; (5) re-estimate the model with least squares on all inliers. The required iterations satisfy N >= log(1-p)/log(1-(1-e)^s) for success probability p, sample size s, and outlier ratio e.

domanda: Explain forward vs inverse warping and the image blending step that follows alignment.
risposta: Forward warping iterates over source pixels, maps each to its new position, and copies the value - but this leaves holes (unfilled destination pixels) and overlaps (several sources mapping to one destination). Inverse warping iterates over destination pixels and uses the inverse transform to find the source location, guaranteeing every output pixel is filled; since the source location is usually non-integer, interpolation (nearest-neighbor, bilinear, bicubic) is needed. After alignment, images are blended: feathering uses a weighted alpha average in the overlap with smoothly transitioning weights (can cause ghosting if misaligned), while pyramid blending merges per frequency band for seamless results.
